originalTitle: Sebi directs depositories to freeze promoter holdings during buyback period, new rules explained
simplifiedContent: The Indian stock market regulator, Sebi, has made a new rule to prevent promoters (the main people in charge of a company) from selling their shares during a buyback period. This means that the promoters' shares will be "frozen" and they won't be able to sell them until the buyback is over. However, promoters can still choose to sell their shares back to the company through a tender offer. This new rule will help ensure that promoters don't take advantage of the buyback process, and it will start being enforced by depositories (the companies that hold the shares) on August 1. This change aims to make the buyback process fairer and more transparent.

originalTitle: London Stock Exchange to start nonstop trading next year
simplifiedContent: The London Stock Exchange is planning to start a new system called LSE 24, which will allow people to buy and sell investments almost all the time. This means that instead of only being able to trade during regular business hours, people will be able to trade at more times of the day. The exchange wants to make it easier for people to trade and to attract more business by offering this new service. This change is partly because younger investors are used to being able to trade digital assets, like cryptocurrencies, at any time. By offering more flexible trading hours, the London Stock Exchange hopes to make trading easier and more attractive to its clients.

originalTitle: Global Market Today: Asian stocks advance on tech rally, yen weakens
simplifiedContent: Here's what's happening in the stock market: stocks in Asia are going up, especially for companies that make computer chips. This is because people are feeling optimistic about investments in artificial intelligence. At the same time, oil prices are rising, which is making people worry about inflation, and the value of the Japanese yen is going down compared to the US dollar. These changes are affecting the prices of other investments like gold, silver, and US government bonds. Now, investors are waiting to see how well two big companies, Alphabet and Tesla, did financially to figure out what might happen next in the market.
